metadata.title: Intel's Comeback Is Being Paid For By Intel

content.text:
Intel's factories are still losing money on wafers they mostly sell to Intel, and the stock's multiple likely assumes that changes.
Intel (INTC) stock has returned 278% over the past year. At about 8.2 times sales it sits in the top decile of its own decade, a price that works only if the factories eventually earn like a business instead of absorbing one. What should worry a holder is what those factories cost right now.
The $2.1 Billion Intel Foundry Lost In A Single Quarter
Intel Foundry, the manufacturing arm, booked $5.8 billion of revenue in the second quarter of 2026 and an operating loss of $2.1 billion. That is most of the $2.5 billion of operating profit the data center AI group produced in the same quarter. Across the trailing twelve months the whole company earns a 7.6% operating margin on $57.0 billion of revenue, a fraction of the roughly 34% margin it earned at its peak, with revenue up 7.5% year over year.
External Customers Were Only $293 Million Of Q2 Foundry Revenue
Just $293 million of the foundry's Q2 2026 revenue came from external customers, roughly 5% of what the segment sold. Nearly all the rest is Intel buying wafers from Intel, so the loss is Intel's own to carry. Wafer costs are improving with higher yields, improved cycle times, and increased factory scale across its leading-edge nodes, and management says the cost of its main Panther Lake part is down roughly 50% year to date, with an additional 20% on track in 2026. By the CFO's own account, Panther Lake and Intel's other newer parts are becoming a significant share of the mix while still sitting below the corporate average margin early in their life cycle.
Capex Above $20 Billion, And Higher Again In 2027
Management is raising 2026 capital spending to more than $20 billion and has said 2027 will run significantly above that. Roughly $30 billion of cash and short-term investments plus a $10 billion revolver cover that bill for now, on top of roughly $10 billion of noncore assets the CFO says could still be monetized, though he has said a ramp as successful as Intel is driving for could still send it to the capital markets. Much of that spending chases one build-out, and the mix already leans that way: AI-driven businesses contributed roughly 70% of revenue in Q2 2026, including record data center growth. Owning the stock here is a bet on that one build-out, a different proposition from the Trefis High Quality Portfolio, which does not depend on the handful of largest technology names to produce its returns.
